# Split Frontend and Backend Hosting

**Decision:** deploy the [[stickfps]] client as a static bundle on one host and the game server as a
long-lived process on another, rather than shipping one application. Recorded as project constraint
C5.

> "Vercel serverless functions time out at 10s and cannot hold a 60Hz authoritative loop — the game
> server needs a persistent process, so it's split out."
> — browser_game_stickfps/PROJECT.md, 2026-07-25

## The reasoning generalises past Vercel

A serverless function is billed and scheduled per request; it has an execution ceiling and no
identity between invocations. An authoritative game server is the opposite on all three axes: it runs
continuously, it *is* the state ([[server-authoritative-netcode]] keeps every `Room` in memory), and
its clock must not be interrupted ([[fixed-timestep-simulation]] at 60 Hz). Nothing about that is
specific to one vendor — it disqualifies the whole serverless execution model, and it also rules out
scaling by replicas without a room-affinity layer that does not exist here.

The client, meanwhile, is the ideal serverless workload: a [[vite]] build with no server-side logic
at all, deployable to any static host or CDN.

Splitting lets each half be hosted on what suits it, and it is what allowed the backend host to be
swapped entirely in [[render-over-fly-io]] without touching the frontend deployment.

## What the split costs

- **Two deployments, in order.** The backend must exist first, because `VITE_*` variables are inlined
  at build time — see [[vite]]. A server URL change is a frontend rebuild.
- **Cross-origin by construction.** The `CORS_ORIGIN` allowlist and the WebSocket `verifyClient`
  origin check exist because of this split ([[ws-websocket-server]]).
- **Two idle behaviours to reason about.** A static bundle is always warm; a free backend instance is
  not ([[render-hosting]]).

## Status

The split is real in the code and in the runbook. Whether both halves were ever deployed together is
the open question on [[stickfps]]: the interview confirms multiplayer play over a real network, while
`docs/DEPLOYMENT.md` states no deploy had been run as of the last commit, and no `render.yaml` or
`vercel.json` exists in the tree. `TODO:` the actual hosts of the live session are unevidenced —
`confidence: low` on that sub-claim; the decision itself is well documented.
